title: GPU runtime profiling - TensorRT-LLM/vLLM/CUDA graphs deep dive
summary: Deep technical session to profile GPU runtime behavior across TensorRT-LLM and vLLM backends; focused on kernel selection, CUDA graphs, KV cache interactions, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, and constraints for Solaris' planned VPC/private deployment. Agreed to run bench with three focal models, share kernel traces and a perf spreadsheet, and schedule a follow-up POC run with dedicated capacity trial.
next_steps: Redwood to share perf spreadsheet and raw kernel traces (Anika)
Solaris to provide target model checkpoints + sample prompt workload (Priya)
Schedule pilot run on Dedicated capacity for end-to-end latency and throughput tests (Miles)
Security: send SOC2/ISO snapshot and KMS integration doc (Lena)
Follow-up call in one week to review results
action_items: Anika Rao | Share perf spreadsheet with kernel-level timings and CUDA graph notes | 2026-03-10
Priya Kapoor | Provide three model checkpoints and 48-hour representative traffic trace | 2026-03-09
Miles Chen | Provision dedicated test nodes and baseline config for pilot | 2026-03-12
Renee Yu | Confirm encryption/KMS requirements and add any compliance constraints | 2026-03-11
transcript:
[00:00] Anika: okay hi everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Anika ra o from Redwood, i'll kick us off. today Miles from infra and Lena from our platform team are with me.
[00:08] Priya: hey thanks, Priya here, excited, we've been wrestling with inconsistent p99s when we push to private clusters, so hoping to get into kernel-level profiling.
[00:16] Miles: hi all, will try to keep this practical — we're going to walk through where TensorRT-LLM and vLLM behave differently and what CUDA graphs buys you.
[00:24] Evan: quick note, we are on-prem in a VPC-isolated colo, NVLink across A100s, and we have mixed gen cards — a few A100s and some L4s for inference.
[00:32] Marco: perf goals: sub-100ms average for 512 tokens, p99 under 350ms, sustain 60 qps with batching.
[00:40] Miles: okay good. first slide — kernel selection. in practice, TensorRT picks fused attention/kernel combos that are highly optimized, but it requires warmup and specific sequence lengths. v L L M on the other hand uses a different kernel set, more permissive, better for variable sequence lengths. sometimes the transcripter says v-l-l-m but, um, we mean vLLM.
[00:57] Priya: does that mean TensorRT will beat vLLM always on latency? we saw better throughput but very uneven tail.
[01:04] Miles: not always. TensorRT-LLM can give lower median latency when the model is supported and you can compile stable CUDA graphs for that seq length. but if your workload has heavy sequence length variance or lots of short/long mixes, the kernel switching and graph reissue cause tails.
[01:20] Evan: graph reissue? explain that — like reconstructing the graph at runtime?
[01:24] Miles: yeah, if your sequence length changes beyond the compiled shape, TensorRT may need to rebuild or fall back, which costs ms and can spike p99s. CUDA graphs help by capturing execution paths, but they are shape-sensitive. if you can bucket your requests into a few fixed shapes, graf graphs (sic) are amazing.
[01:40] Priya: OK — what about KV cache behaviors? we rely heavily on long context reuse for assistant sessions.
[01:44] Lena: KV cache in vLLM is very explicit — continuous caching of key/value tensors and reusing them is relatively straightforward; vLLM has really good cache locality for autoregressive workloads. TensorRT-LLM can also do KV caching but kernel fusions sometimes expect certain memory layouts and pack the KV differently which affects cache hits.
[02:02] Marco: so we'd see different memory pressure patterns? we already hit OOM on some of our A100 nodes when batching.
[02:07] Miles: yes. TensorRT fused kernels sometimes allocate transient buffers that inflate peak memory; vLLM tends to have more granular allocations but potentially more memcpy overhead. quantization helps a lot — int8 or 4-bit reduces KV footprint, but accuracy regen (sic) needs validation.
[02:24] Priya: how stable is 4-bit quant for our family of models? we use an Llama-2 13B variant and a custom Llama mix.
[02:31] Anika: we should run quality evals; quantization profiles vary. in our experience, symmetric 4-bit with per-channel scales works pretty good for chatty models, but you need calibration prompts and eval sets. we'll share our quant notes.
[02:41] Evan: latency vs cost tradeoff — if we go 4-bit on L4-class cards versus fp16 on A100, what's the ballpark?
[02:47] Miles: ballpark — 4-bit on L4 might give similar token throughput to fp16 on A100 for short sequences, but long-context and KV-heavy sessions may still prefer A100 fp16 for stability. cost modeling is complex; our Optimize team has heuristics.
[03:00] Speaker 1: (interruption) sorry slight audio glitch.
[03:05] Miles: no worries. next, batching. continuous batching in Redwood groups concurrent requests into microbatches; kernel selection depends on batch size and seq len. larger batches improve throughput but can add latency for the first request. so we support dynamic batching with latency SLO controls.
[03:22] Priya: for our target 60 qps, what's the sweet spot for batch sizes on A100?
[03:26] Miles: empirically, for 13B models with 512 tokens, we saw best throughput around batch sizes 16-32 on A100 with TensorRT-LLM and batch 8-16 on vLLM for more predictable tails. tokenization patterns and prompt prefixes affect it.
[03:40] Marco: can we simulate that with our traces? we want to see p50/p95/p99 across bucketed shapes.
[03:45] Anika: yes, provide us the traces, we'll run parallel profiles and return kernel traces and timeline flame graphs.
[03:51] Priya: perfect. 
[03:54] Miles: about profiling artifacts — we'll produce CUDA kernel timelines, nvprof-like summaries, and TensorRT engine logs. note that some names in the logs are obfuscated or simplified — the label mapping can be tricky, we'll include a legend.
[04:08] Evan: on VPC/on-prem constraints: our security team insists on no outbound control plane traffic and on KMS within our VPC. how does Redwood handle that?
[04:16] Lena: Redwood Private supports a customer-managed control plane; we've done air-gapped installs. we also have KMS integrations with customer HSMs, but some runtime telemetry requires a restricted channel; we can mute or ship logs to a customer S3. we'll follow up with the KMS integration doc.
[04:33] Renee: yes please. encryption at rest and audit logs are non-negotiable. also need RBAC and SSO.
[04:38] Anika: understood, Lena will send SOC2 snapshot and SAML integration notes.
[04:42] Marco: deeper on CUDA graphs — how do you manage multiple shapes without rebuilding graphs constantly?
[04:47] Miles: common approach is shape bucketing: pick a small set of representative (batch, seq) shapes and compile a graph per bucket. route requests to nearest bucket; small padding may be required and KV caching must be aligned to bucket shapes. we also sometimes fallback to a vLLM runtime for oddball shapes to avoid rebuilds.
[05:03] Priya: what's the overhead of padding to a bucket? if we pad a lot we waste compute.
[05:07] Miles: yes padding overhead shows up as additional tokens processed; tradeoff is between wasted FLOPs and rebuild latency. for conversational workloads with many short queries, smaller buckets with low padding are better. for long-context tasks, fewer bigger buckets may be fine. we'll show examples in the perf sheets.
[05:23] Anika: quick demo — we have two micro-recordings: one where we run 13B on TensorRT with graphs and one on vLLM. i'll narrate.
[05:31] (screen share)
[05:35] Miles: look at this kernel timeline — see periodic spikes at 2.3s, that's graph recompile on shape mismatch. also the attention kernel here (labelled fmha_gemm in the trace) takes a variable amount depending on sequence length. on vLLM the attention kernel is more consistent but there is higher memcpy time into the batch buffer.
[05:55] Priya: hm the labels fmha_gemm look unfamiliar, is that from TRT or cuDNN?
[05:58] Miles: it's a fused attention kernel name from our tracing layer, underneath it's usually TensorRT/cuda conv/epilogue kernels. names can be weird in the nvtx output.
[06:07] Marco: can you produce a per-kernel time csv so we can plug into our cost model?
[06:10] Anika: yes will include per-kernel CSV and an annotated timeline GIF.
[06:15] Priya: any gotchas with mixed gen GPUs? we have A100 and L4 in same cluster.
[06:20] Miles: heterogeneous clusters complicate kernel selection; TensorRT engines are usually built for a compute capability; you might need separate engine pools per GPU type. our smart routing can direct workloads to compatible pools, but it increases operational surface.
[06:34] Evan: can we offload some infers to L4 for non-critical traffic to save cost?
[06:37] Miles: yes, with model variants (smaller quantized versions) or lower precision, you can route best-effort traffic to L4s. Redwood routing policies support that.
[06:45] Priya: about accuracy regressions with quant — how do we guard against regressions in rollouts?
[06:49] Anika: Redwood Optimize ties evals to deployments; we do A/B rollouts and run automated eval sets on canaries. we'll share the eval harness.
[06:57] Marco: curious: what's the time-to-compile for a TensorRT engine and then for its graph on a 13B?
[07:02] Miles: compile time varies — engine building can be minutes to tens of minutes depending on workspace size and tactic cache hits; graph capture is quick once engine loaded, but if you need calibrations for int8 it can add time. plan for a few hours for full production tuning if you want optimized fp16+int8 kernels.
[07:21] Priya: that's longer than we'd hoped but manageable.
[07:24] Anika: one more point — warmup. warmup traffic to populate KV cache and JIT caches significantly lowers first-request latency. for steady-state it's negligible but for bursty cold starts it matters.
[07:36] Evan: what about prewarming across N nodes? we have burst windows.
[07:39] Miles: we can orchestrate warmup jobs that replay representative traces; for Dedicated we can reserve burst capacity.
[07:46] Priya: okay let's talk experiments — we want: 1) baseline fp16 vLLM, 2) TensorRT fp16 with graphs for 3 buckets, 3) quantized INT8/4-bit evaluation on both runtimes. 4) Dedicated run in our VPC.
[08:00] Anika: sounds good. we'll need your traces and checkpoints.
[08:03] Priya: i'll get them over.
[08:05] (cross talk: names confirm)
[08:10] Miles: final notes — we'll include a mapping from engine logs to kernel labels, and a section on memory footprint per kernel so you can predict OOMs. also will call out tuning knobs: tactic cache, workspace size, cudnn autotune flags.
[08:24] Marco: great. any concerns about licensing or export controls for TensorRT engines?
[08:29] Lena: typically no, but some gov customers request local-only builds; we can accommodate.
[08:33] Priya: thanks everyone — recap and next steps?
[08:36] Anika: recap: Redwood to run parallel profiles once you send model/checkpoints and traces; we'll share kernel-level CSVs, CUDA timelines, quantization notes, and KMS/SOC2 docs. schedule follow-up next week.
[08:48] Evan: thanks.
[08:49] Priya: thanks all.
[08:52] (meeting ends)
